clue.text: Make particular study of plaice varying in dimensions

indicators.note: in places the shuffled fish inside the word for dimensions

parts.note: size means dimensions, the measurements of a thing

indicators.note: varying tells us the letters of plaice change their order

explanation.surface: Someone is making a detailed study of how flatfish differ in size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plaice' pulls toward fish, but it is only anagram fodder; 'varying' shuffles it and 'in' sets it within the word for dimensions, split after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To specialize is to concentrate one's study on a single particular field.

clue.text: Criticize the German procurer.

parts.note: to pan is to criticize harshly
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: Someone criticizes a German pimp.
explanation.definitionFit: A pander is a pimp or go-between who supplies others' lusts.

clue.text: Company present not disheartened, sticking together

parts.note: here means present, in attendance

indicators.note: disheartened means the middle of the word not is removed

explanation.surface: The firm's staff are there, but not in good spirits, while holding together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' removes the O from NOT, leaving NT.
explanation.definitionFit: A coherent argument is logically consistent, its parts holding firmly united.

clue.text: Martin's novel job, making bolts at the forge?

definitions.meaning: Sinclair Lewis's novel about the doctor Martin of that surname

definitions.text: job, making bolts at the forge
definitions.meaning: a smith who forges arrowheads, bolts being crossbow arrows

explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair Lewis's 1925 novel is named for its hero, and the same word names a maker of arrowheads.

clue.text: Sluggishness of train — that's strange

indicators.note: strange signals the letters are put in an unusual order

parts.note: IE, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A slow train is unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges TRAIN plus IE, the abbreviation for 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertia is a lack of motion or energy, a tendency to stay still.

clue.text: Fine picture contains a poem

indicators.note: contains tells us the answer is held within the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A good painting includes a verse.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a long narrative poem about heroic deeds.

clue.text: Dim spy may thus make tactless remark

parts.note: to blur is to dim or obscure
a tout spies on racehorses in training

explanation.surface: A dull secret agent might say something indiscreet.
explanation.walkthrough: A racing tout watches training gallops to get tips, hence spy.
explanation.definitionFit: To blurt out is to say something suddenly and without thought, often indiscreetly.

clue.text: "The — and rose of the fair state" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "The — and rose of the fair state" (Hamlet)

parts.words: "The — and rose of the fair state" (Hamlet)
parts.note: Ophelia's line praising Hamlet as the hope and flower of Denmark, with one word blank

explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia calls Hamlet the hope and bloom of the realm; the missing word means that anticipation.

clue.text: Long-winded expert is given £9

parts.note: a pro is an expert, a professional
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra
IX is nine in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A verbose specialist is paid a modest fee of nine pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR lost the pound sign; the page prints £9, giving L (pound) and IX (nine).
explanation.definitionFit: Prolix speech or writing uses far too many words, so it is wordy and tedious.

clue.text: Having been apprehended like the boss?

definitions.meaning: taken ... is an old police phrase for arrested
the boss is the one who runs things, holding command

explanation.definitionFit: Being taken in charge means arrest by police, while a person in charge is the one with authority.

clue.text: Training for sappers in this resort

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, are the British Army's sappers
a course is a programme of training

explanation.surface: An army engineering unit runs its training at a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday town, but it means a last resort, something to fall back on.
explanation.definitionFit: Having recourse to something means turning to it for help, as a fallback or source of aid.

clue.text: Such as the translation we don't pay for?

definitions.text: Such as the translation we don't pay for?

parts.words: Such as the translation we don't pay for?
parts.note: two senses fused: a loose rendering of a text, and something that costs nothing

explanation.definitionFit: A loose, non-literal translation carries this name, and anything costing nothing gets the same adjective.

clue.text: Maybe half California it took in, to make it easy

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be otherwise, so they are rearranged
half takes only the first half of the ten-letter state name

parts.note: taken as written
to eat is to take in food, so took in means ate

explanation.surface: Perhaps half of California swallowed something so as to ease things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes the first five letters of California, and 'Maybe' shuffles them; 'it' then stands as written and 'took in' means consumed.
explanation.definitionFit: To facilitate a task is to smooth its way, helping it proceed more simply.

clue.text: Dicky's a false one!

parts.note: a dicky is a detachable panel worn to look like the front of a shirt

explanation.definitionFit: A dicky is a separate starched panel worn under a jacket in place of a full shirt's front.

clue.text: Not reaching the boundary, but over the half century

definitions.meaning: in cricket a hit that falls short of the boundary rope may score three runs rather than four

explanation.definitionFit: A cricket stroke short of the rope may yield a three, and the word also means sixty, above fifty.

clue.text: A little witchcraft can make one fall

parts.note: taken as written
a trip is a stumble or fall

explanation.surface: A minor spell can make someone stumble.
explanation.walkthrough: CANTRIP is a Scots word for a magic spell or trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantrip is a small charm or spell, a piece of minor sorcery.

clue.text: Maid's 12ac time a clue for "thing"

parts.note: the letters of night, put out of order, would make the word thing

explanation.surface: A servant's evening off is offered as a hint for some word.
explanation.walkthrough: 12ac is FREE: a maid's free time is her evening off. Read as wordplay, NIGHT with OUT as anagram signal gives THING.
explanation.definitionFit: Domestic servants were given an evening away from work, their free evening.

clue.text: Made continued progress, we hear, in Lancashire?

indicators.note: we hear tells us the phrase is spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: pressed on means kept going forward

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether progress was made somewhere in Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: PRESTON is a town in Lancashire, a county in north-west England; the definition is a place found there.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston is the administrative centre of the county in north-west England, so it lies within it.

clue.text: Grabs poles — cheats abominably

parts.note: S and N are the south and north poles

indicators.note: abominably means badly, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone seizes Polish people and cheats them terribly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poles' is not about Polish people: it gives south and north; 'abominably' then shuffles the word cheats to follow them.
explanation.definitionFit: To snatch is to seize quickly, so snatches means grabs.

clue.text: Act like one, on board, to promote another

definitions.meaning: to behave like a royal consort, haughtily
in chess a pawn reaching the last rank is promoted to the strongest piece

explanation.definitionFit: To lord it over others like royalty, and in chess to turn a pawn into the most powerful piece.

clue.text: It makes Sheila tough (without a sailors' warning)

indicators.note: makes signals the letters are worked into something new
without tells us a letter from the phrase is left out

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something hardens a woman called Sheila, who gets no seaman's caution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' takes A out of SHEILA TOUGH, leaving SHEILTOUGH, and 'makes' rearranges those ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tower with a lamp alerts ships to rocks and shoals, a warning for seafarers.

clue.text: Friend who's an entirely unknown quantity

parts.note: all can mean entirely, as in all alone
in algebra y is an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: A companion is someone we know nothing at all about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unknown quantity' is the crossword convention for X, Y or Z from algebra.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally is a supporter who sides with you, a companion in a cause.

clue.text: Pulse fast? Over one-fifty

indicators.note: over places the first piece above the next in this down entry

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting
I is the Roman numeral one
L is the Roman numeral fifty

explanation.surface: Is a heartbeat racing at more than one hundred and fifty?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' looks like a heartbeat, but it is a bean or edible seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Lentils are legumes, and pulses are the dried edible seeds of such plants.

clue.text: Mickey taken by one bird or another

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
Mickey is the famous cartoon mouse

explanation.surface: Mickey Mouse is carried off by some bird or other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken by' joins the pieces, the mouse going after the bird; 'another' then names a second bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The titmouse is a further small songbird, a fuller name for the tit family.

clue.text: Kind of turn going on first in the Hebrides

indicators.note: going on means the second piece is placed after the first

parts.note: a U-turn is a kind of turn
1st, written with I standing for the figure one

explanation.surface: Some sort of turning is happening first in the Scottish islands.
explanation.walkthrough: UIST is an island in the Outer Hebrides, off Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: North and South Uist are islands in the Outer Hebrides chain.

clue.text: They open badly for the beginner

indicators.note: badly signals the letters are put in a disordered arrangement

explanation.surface: Novices tend to make a poor start.
explanation.definitionFit: A neophyte is a novice or recent convert, someone new to a field.

clue.text: Fanfares in clubs, for instance

definitions.meaning: an old word for trumpet blasts
in card games the suit ranked above the rest, of which clubs may be one

explanation.definitionFit: Trumpet calls were once called this, and in cards the winning suit, such as clubs, carries the same name.

clue.text: Auctioneer lets everything rip!

parts.note: tatters are rags or rips, torn pieces
all means everything

explanation.surface: An auctioneer lets the bidding go wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Tattersalls is the famous horse auctioneer at Newmarket; 'lets' links, the pieces read in reverse order.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Tattersall founded the bloodstock auction house, so the name stands for the auctioneer.
